ESIDIMENI WRAP HEARING

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Qedani Mahlangu on the stand -- we capture the fury and fire around the most-anticipated testimony of the Esidimeni Arbitration hearings.

Unique Selling Point:
It's the moment that hundreds of families and survivors of the Esidimeni tragedy have collectively been holding their breaths for.

Will former Gauteng Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu take the stand, as she's undertaken to do, since initially dodging calls for her to appear last year?

Will she have a breakdown after her first day -- as did one of her officials Dr Makgabo Manamela, who failed to take any real responsibility for the disaster under her watch?

Or will Mahlangu finally come clean -- acknowledging the culture of intimidation and coercion that was hinted at by loyal cadre erstwhile Department head Dr Barney Selebano as well as state witness Levy Mosenogi, the Gauteng Health Department Chief Director of planning, policy and research who earlier in proceedings had broken down, in a display of grief and brokenness, and admitted to bowing to the pressure exerted by the former MEC?

Selebano's testimony ended the year's hearings in floods of tears as he pleaded for forgiveness from families while on social media, where the hearings are streamed live, he was crucified as insincere and his testimony, as only half the story.

We recap the key problem areas that have emerged from the the hearings -- and follow the moments surrounding Mahlangu's appearance.

Press Release:


Former Gauteng Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu was finally in the hot seat at the Life Esidimeni Arbitration hearings this week where she apologised to families of victims of the tragedy. But in her testimony, she took no responsibility and shifted blame to then suspended Gauteng Health Department head Barney Selebano and Mental Health director, Dr Makgabo Manamela, both of whom had recently resigned from their posts. Meanwhile, affected families still need real answers and the big question remains: who will take ultimate responsibility for the tragic deaths of 143 mentally ill state patients?

Script:


INSERT:

DEVI LINK: Over 51 days since October last year, families have sat in the Esidimeni Arbitration hearings for answers -- WHO made the decisions that ended in 143 of their loved ones dead...many traumatised...and almost 60 still unaccounted for?

VO: Andrew Petersen comes to hear why his uncle Victor Truter who has schizophrenia, and who was stable after 40 years at Life Esidimeni, had his life and fragile health turned upside down by a move to a small NGO.

ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: He didn’t get his medication for something like two weeks. He wasn’t getting food and he wasn’t getting water. Now he’s doing much better.

VO: Carte Blanche sought answers when the first deaths came to light.

(STRAP Interview August 2016) DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: We have a few relapsed cases…QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG MEC FOR HEALTH: I do not remember any information…DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER: Since June? Nothing? QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER GAUTENG MEC FOR HEALTH: …of any patients relapsing in this.

VO: Then MEC Qedani Mahlangu claimed they wanted to save money; deinstitutionalise mental health care; and open up a contract monopolised for decades by one service provider -- LIFE ESIDIMENI. Chronic psychiatric patients had to be housed elsewhere.

DEVI LINK: NGOs were totally unprepared for the burden of care -- from this room a picture has emerged of political strong-arming to RUSH through a relocation project so disorganised, it robbed patients of all dignity.

ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: I went there on the day. The whole situation was chaotic. Patients were sitting around all over the place. It was shambolic. I mean, boxes of files were carried haphazardly to and fro…even the drivers couldn’t tell us where they were taking my uncle.

VO: The NGOs did not get their subsidies or support from the department and patients were left starving and freezing. Medical ethics professor Ames Dhai studied the death certificates and the health ombudsman’s report on the tragedy.

PROF. AMES DHAI, DIRECTOR, STEVE BIKO CENTRE FOR BIOETHICS, WITS: The patients were not treated as patients. They were treated as individuals of a lower moral standing. They lacked human dignity. So they were exploited. And when you look at how black
people were treated before 1994, you ask yourself, in certain sectors what has really changed?

VO: In the Gauteng Health Department, a handful of people carried ultimate responsibility for moving a thousand-seven hundred patients. One after another, the officials came before retired Judge Dikgang Moseneke at the hearings and pointed fingers to the top. Levy Mosenogi, then chief planning director, was given three months to get the mammoth move done.

LEVY MOSENOGI, PLANNING DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: I realised it was too short a time.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: But why? What was the urgency about?
LEVY MOSENOGI, PLANNING DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: In my opinion, it was because they had already written to Life and terminated the contract. I can’t explain the urgency in terms of why did we have to close ... those were the timeframes I was given and …
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Timeframes given to you by whom?
LEVY MOSENOGI, PLANNING DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: HOD and MEC, Dr Selebano and Miss Qedani Mahlangu.

VO: Hannah Jacobus, then a deputy director responsible for NGOs, admitted to writing out the licences for the NGOs even though she knew they had not been properly assessed.

HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: Manamela said we have to do it because it’s an instruction from above and all orders has to be carried out.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Well, let’s be a bit dramatic about this -- I instruct you to murder Advocate Groenewald. Do you oblige? What’s your answer?
HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: No, Justice.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: No, you wouldn’t do it, would you? Why wouldn’t you do it?
HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: Because it’s against the law to do that.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: The irony does not escape you, does it?
HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: No, Justice.

VO: Dr. Makgabo Manamela was director for mental health and Jacobus’ boss.

JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Why did you start a project when you have not prepared for it?
DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: The termination notice was given to Life Esidimeni by the executive and we were clearly informed that by that time we need to have placed the patients.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Which senior of you gave you the instructions?
DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: The MEC and the HOD.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Did you know how bad things were at NGOs?
DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: After we placed the patients, I knew, I knew how bad situation were in some of the NGOs.

VO: Dr. Barney Selebano was the head of the department and the most senior official below the MEC. He admitted to backdating a licence to validate an NGO.

DR BARNEY SELEBANO, FORMER HEAD OF DEPARTMENT, GAUTENG HEALTH: We did everything wrong, very wrong by not heeding to advice, not listening to other people.

VO: Selebano got the call from health minister Aaron Motsoaledi to close down the deathtrap NGOs when news of the deaths emerged.

DEVI LINK: This week, the arrival of former health MEC Qedani Mahlangu drew angry crowds. Inside, the families greeted her with an old anti-apartheid song which asks: What have we done to deserve this?

QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: The deaths of approximately 140 mental health care users is indeed painful and regrettable. Clearly this did not go according to plan and for that I sincerely apologise.

DEVI LINK: For every finger pointing at Mahlangu she pointed back at officials.

QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: To say that the decision was Qedani Mahlangu, I think it would be misleading the public. The decision in government is never an individual decision. It was our collective decision as a department.
JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Who were in the collective?
QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: It was myself, the HOD and all of us in meeting… I had full confidence in the managers.

JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Why did you not open the door of the MEC and say I am not going to authorise this any further?
DR BARNEY SELEBANO, FORMER HEAD OF DEPARTMENT, GAUTENG HEALTH: There was no space. There’s no space to differ sharply…There’s no space. If you start differing with your leader you must know the relationship is going to be extremely difficult.

VO: In desperation, Mosenogi wrote to Mahlangu warning about problems and asking for an extension. She testified that she was being treated for back problems at the time -- she didn’t recall seeing the letter. We know that by the time Mahlangu told the legislature in September 2016 that 36 patients had died, the number was already double that. But she maintained she simply didn’t know...

QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER MEC FOR HEALTH, GAUTENG: Once I got to know about the problems, things became a bit difficult and tense in the department, and of course levels of trust degenerated. Why they didn’t inform me that there were challenges of payments and things... I wouldn’t know why information was withheld from me.

DEVI LINK: It’s up to Moseneke to decide who to believe and to recommend further steps.

VO: Family members have heard many apologies over the last few months, but Mahlangu left them cold.

ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: We’re not happy that she hasn’t been forthcoming and that’s been a lot of finger pointing which is very painful for the families. So we need to forgive them for us to find healing. But we can’t forgive them if they’re not prepared to repent.

QEDANI MAHLANGU: I served in a public office and I assumed political responsibility and I cannot carry personal blame because I was not working for my personal self.

PROF. AMES DHAI, DIRECTOR, STEVE BIKO CENTRE FOR BIOETHICS, WITS: When she was sworn in, she had to take an oath or a solemn declaration that she would protect and honour our Constitution, she would conduct her affairs with integrity and dignity and honesty. Now when you look at how she’s conducted herself, she’s done none of this. She has disgraced her office.

VO: Mahlangu, Selebano and Manamela have all resigned, getting off without disciplinary action and with their pensions intact. Mosenogi and Jacobus still work in the department.

PROF. AMES DHAI, DIRECTOR, STEVE BIKO CENTRE FOR BIOETHICS, WITS: When you look at the healthcare professionals in terms of their responsibilities as officials it was very, very clear that they had totally disregarded their oaths that they had taken as healthcare professionals. They were morally wrong in their conduct and in this way wronged the patients.

HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: I really apologise to the families and I’m really extremely, extremely sorry that I’ve allowed management to bully me to continue implementing this. So for my part, and my guilt feelings, I don’t know whether I’ll ever be able to get rid of that. And I just pray and ask that people will pray with me.

LEVY MOSENOGI, PLANNING DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: I would like to say there were lessons that we learned. The lesson is that we need all the time to speak truth to power.


PROMOS
10 secs
Unwilling to take personal responsibility for the Life Esidimeni tragedy … will the families of victims ever forgive former Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu?

15 secs
For every finger pointed at Qedani Mahlangu as the force behind the Life Esidimeni tragedy, she fingers officials who’ve now resigned...what will the arbitration process bring?
QEDANI MAHLANGU: The decision in government is never an individual decision. It was our collective decision...

15 secs
Families of the Life Esidimeni victims expected former MEC Qedani Mahlangu to help them understand what happened, but will they accept her answers?
ANDREW PETERSEN: We need to forgive them for us to find healing. But we can’t forgive them if they’re not prepared to repent.

DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: Because it’s against the law to do that. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: The irony does not escape you, does it? HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: No, Justice. VO: Dr. Makgabo Manamela was director for mental health and Jacobus’ boss. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Why did you start a project when you have not prepared for it? DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: The termination notice was given to Life Esidimeni by the executive and we were clearly informed that by that time we need to have placed the patients. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Which senior of you gave you the instructions? DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: The MEC and the HOD. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Did you know how bad things were at NGOs? DR MAKGABO MANAMELA, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: After we placed the patients, I knew, I knew how bad situation were in some of the NGOs. VO: Dr. Barney Selebano was the head of the department and the most senior official below the MEC. He admitted to backdating a licence to validate an NGO. DR BARNEY SELEBANO, FORMER HEAD OF DEPARTMENT, GAUTENG HEALTH: We did everything wrong, very wrong by not heeding to advice, not listening to other people. VO: Selebano got the call from health minister Aaron Motsoaledi to close down the deathtrap NGOs when news of the deaths emerged. DEVI LINK: This week, the arrival of former health MEC Qedani Mahlangu drew angry crowds. Inside, the families greeted her with an old anti-apartheid song which asks: What have we done to deserve this? QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: The deaths of approximately 140 mental health care users is indeed painful and regrettable. Clearly this did not go according to plan and for that I sincerely apologise. DEVI LINK: For every finger pointing at Mahlangu she pointed back at officials. QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: To say that the decision was Qedani Mahlangu, I think it would be misleading the public. The decision in government is never an individual decision. It was our collective decision as a department. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Who were in the collective? QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER HEALTH MEC, GAUTENG: It was myself, the HOD and all of us in meeting… I had full confidence in the managers. JUSTICE DIKGANG MOSENEKE: Why did you not open the door of the MEC and say I am not going to authorise this any further? DR BARNEY SELEBANO, FORMER HEAD OF DEPARTMENT, GAUTENG HEALTH: There was no space. There’s no space to differ sharply…There’s no space. If you start differing with your leader you must know the relationship is going to be extremely difficult. VO: In desperation, Mosenogi wrote to Mahlangu warning about problems and asking for an extension. She testified that she was being treated for back problems at the time -- she didn’t recall seeing the letter. We know that by the time Mahlangu told the legislature in September 2016 that 36 patients had died, the number was already double that. But she maintained she simply didn’t know... QEDANI MAHLANGU, FORMER MEC FOR HEALTH, GAUTENG: Once I got to know about the problems, things became a bit difficult and tense in the department, and of course levels of trust degenerated. Why they didn’t inform me that there were challenges of payments and things... I wouldn’t know why information was withheld from me. DEVI LINK: It’s up to Moseneke to decide who to believe and to recommend further steps. VO: Family members have heard many apologies over the last few months, but Mahlangu left them cold. ANDREW PETERSEN, FAMILY COMMITTEE MEMBER: We’re not happy that she hasn’t been forthcoming and that’s been a lot of finger pointing which is very painful for the families. So we need to forgive them for us to find healing. But we can’t forgive them if they’re not prepared to repent. QEDANI MAHLANGU: I served in a public office and I assumed political responsibility and I cannot carry personal blame because I was not working for my personal self. PROF. AMES DHAI, DIRECTOR, STEVE BIKO CENTRE FOR BIOETHICS, WITS: When she was sworn in, she had to take an oath or a solemn declaration that she would protect and honour our Constitution, she would conduct her affairs with integrity and dignity and honesty. Now when you look at how she’s conducted herself, she’s done none of this. She has disgraced her office. VO: Mahlangu, Selebano and Manamela have all resigned, getting off without disciplinary action and with their pensions intact. Mosenogi and Jacobus still work in the department. PROF. AMES DHAI, DIRECTOR, STEVE BIKO CENTRE FOR BIOETHICS, WITS: When you look at the healthcare professionals in terms of their responsibilities as officials it was very, very clear that they had totally disregarded their oaths that they had taken as healthcare professionals. They were morally wrong in their conduct and in this way wronged the patients. HANNAH JACOBUS, DEP. DIRECTOR, MENTAL HEALTH DIRECTORATE, GAUTENG HEALTH: I really apologise to the families and I’m really extremely, extremely sorry that I’ve allowed management to bully me to continue implementing this. So for my part, and my guilt feelings, I don’t know whether I’ll ever be able to get rid of that. And I just pray and ask that people will pray with me. LEVY MOSENOGI, PLANNING DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH: I would like to say there were lessons that we learned. The lesson is that we need all the time to speak truth to power. QEDANI MAHLANGU: The decision in government is never an individual decision. It was our collective decision... 15 secs Families of the Life Esidimeni victims expected former MEC Qedani Mahlangu to help them understand what happened, but will they accept her answers? ANDREW PETERSEN: We need to forgive them for us to find healing. But we can’t forgive them if they’re not prepared to repent.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Qedani Mahlangu on the stand -- we capture the fury and fire around the most-anticipated testimony of the Esidimeni Arbitration hearings.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's the moment that hundreds of families and survivors of the Esidimeni tragedy have collectively been holding their breaths for. Will former Gauteng Health MEC Qedani Mahlangu take the stand, as she's undertaken to do, since initially dodging calls for her to appear last year? Will she have a breakdown after her first day -- as did one of her officials Dr Makgabo Manamela, who failed to take any real responsibility for the disaster under her watch? Or will Mahlangu finally come clean -- acknowledging the culture of intimidation and coercion that was hinted at by loyal cadre erstwhile Department head Dr Barney Selebano as well as state witness Levy Mosenogi, the Gauteng Health Department Chief Director of planning, policy and research who earlier in proceedings had broken down, in a display of grief and brokenness, and admitted to bowing to the pressure exerted by the former MEC? Selebano's testimony ended the year's hearings in floods of tears as he pleaded for forgiveness from families while on social media, where the hearings are streamed live, he was crucified as insincere and his testimony, as only half the story. We recap the key problem areas that have emerged from the the hearings -- and follow the moments surrounding Mahlangu's appearance.
